fields.meta_title: Who Is the Holy Spirit? Understanding the Third Person of God
fields.description: Many Christians find the Holy Spirit the most mysterious part of God. Here is who the Holy Spirit is, what he does, and how to walk with him day by day.
fields.body_html:
Most Christians can say something about God the Father and God the Son. The Holy Spirit is where many grow vague — a force, an influence, a feeling in a worship song. Yet Jesus spoke of the Spirit as the greatest gift he could leave his followers, and the whole life of the church runs on him. So who exactly is the Holy Spirit? Not a what but a who — and knowing him changes everything about how you live the Christian life.

The Holy Spirit is a Person, not a force

The first and most important thing to correct is the instinct to call the Spirit “it.” The Bible never does. Jesus consistently calls the Spirit “he,” and describes him doing personal things — teaching, guiding, comforting, grieving. “When the Spirit of truth comes, he will guide you into all the truth … he will speak” (John 16:13). You can grieve him: “do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God” (Ephesians 4:30) — you cannot grieve a force, only a person who loves you. R. A. Torrey, who wrote two of the clearest books ever penned on the subject — The Person and Work of the Holy Spirit and The Baptism with the Holy Spirit — argued that this single correction transforms the Christian life: the goal is not to get more of an influence, but to be possessed and led by a divine Person who already indwells us.

The Holy Spirit is God

The Spirit is not a junior member of God or a created being; he is fully God, the third Person of the one Trinity. When Peter confronts Ananias for lying “to the Holy Spirit,” he says in the same breath, “You have not lied to man but to God” (Acts 5:3–4) — to lie to the Spirit is to lie to God, because the Spirit is God. He was there at creation, “hovering over the face of the waters” (Genesis 1:2), and he shares the one divine name into which every believer is baptized: “the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 28:19). So to have the Spirit is not to have a lesser blessing than having Christ; it is to have God himself living inside you.

What the Holy Spirit does

The Spirit’s work is vast, but a few strands run through it all. He is, first, the one who gives spiritual life — no one is born again except by the Spirit (John 3:6). Then, in the believer, he takes up residence: “your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit within you, whom you have from God” (1 Corinthians 6:19). Consider that: the God of the universe does not merely visit his people; he moves in.

From within, the Spirit does the work Jesus promised. He is our Helper — “I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Helper, to be with you forever, even the Spirit of truth” (John 14:16–17). He teaches, opening the Scriptures and guiding us into truth (John 16:13). He empowers us to witness: “you will receive power when the Holy Spirit has come upon you” (Acts 1:8). He helps us pray when words fail: “the Spirit helps us in our weakness … the Spirit himself intercedes for us” (Romans 8:26). And over time he changes our character, growing in us “the fruit of the Spirit” — “love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, self-control” (Galatians 5:22–23). Catherine Booth, preaching on The Holy Ghost, pressed the church to see that its weakness was almost always an unclaimed reliance on this very power.

The Spirit and spiritual gifts

The same Spirit who grows this fruit also distributes gifts — abilities given to believers to build up the church and serve others. “To each is given the manifestation of the Spirit for the common good” (1 Corinthians 12:7). Every Christian has at least one such gift, and the Spirit “apportions to each one individually as he wills” (1 Corinthians 12:11). It is worth holding two things together here. The gifts matter — they are how the Spirit equips ordinary people to do more than they could on their own. But Scripture is emphatic that the fruit matters more than the gifts, because gifts without love are noise (1 Corinthians 13:1). A church hungry for the Spirit’s power should be at least as hungry for his character. The Spirit gives gifts to serve; he grows fruit to make us like Christ; and he means for the two to travel together.

Common confusions about the Spirit

Two mistakes are worth naming. The first is to reduce the Spirit to a feeling — to assume he is present only when the emotions run high, and absent in the dry seasons. But the Spirit indwells every believer permanently; his presence is a fact to be trusted, not a mood to be chased. The second is to treat him as an optional extra for advanced Christians. He is not. There is no Christian life at all without the Spirit — “anyone who does not have the Spirit of Christ does not belong to him” (Romans 8:9). The question is never whether a believer has the Spirit, but whether the Spirit fully has the believer.

Why the Spirit is such good news

Think about what this means for ordinary Christian living. You are not left to imitate Jesus from a distance by willpower. The same Spirit who raised Christ from the dead lives in you to produce his life through you. Holiness is not you straining to be good; it is the Spirit bearing his fruit as you yield to him. Understanding is not you cleverly decoding the Bible; it is the Spirit illuminating it. Prayer is not you shouting into silence; it is the Spirit carrying your groans to the Father. The Christian life was never meant to be lived on your own resources — and by the Spirit, it does not have to be.

This also reframes what many find most discouraging about following Jesus: the gap between the person they want to be and the person they are. The Spirit is God’s answer to that gap. He is not a demanding overseer standing over you with a checklist; he is a patient Helper working within you, changing your desires from the inside so that obedience slowly becomes something you want rather than merely something you must. Paul calls this being transformed “from one degree of glory to another. For this comes from the Lord who is the Spirit” (2 Corinthians 3:18). You are not stuck. The very presence of God is at work in you, and he does not abandon what he begins.

How to walk with the Holy Spirit

If the Spirit is a Person who indwells you, then the goal is a relationship, not a technique. A few ways to live in step with him:

  • Depend on him consciously. Begin the day acknowledging that you cannot live it in your own strength, and asking the Spirit to fill and lead you. Paul commands it: “be filled with the Spirit” (Ephesians 5:18) — a continual yielding, not a one-time event.
  • Walk by the Spirit. “Walk by the Spirit, and you will not gratify the desires of the flesh” (Galatians 5:16). Holiness comes not by white-knuckled effort but by moment-by-moment reliance on him.
  • Don’t grieve him. Because he is a Person who loves you, unrepented sin wounds the relationship (Ephesians 4:30). Keep short accounts; confession keeps the fellowship warm.
  • Feed on the Word he inspired. The Spirit and the Scripture always agree; the mind soaked in the Bible is the mind he most readily leads.
  • Ask. “How much more will the heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to those who ask him!” (Luke 11:13). He delights to answer.

If all of this feels like a lot to take in, do not turn it into one more thing to master. The heart of walking with the Spirit is simply this: treat him as the ever-present Person he is. Talk to him. Rely on him before you act. Thank him when you sense his help, and turn back to him quickly when you fail. The Christian who learns to say, a hundred times a day, “Holy Spirit, I need you — lead me,” is learning the whole secret. He is not a reward for the spiritually advanced; he is the constant companion of every ordinary believer, given precisely so that no Christian ever has to face a single hour alone.

The Holy Spirit is not the vague, impersonal part of God. He is God himself, come to live in ordinary people — to comfort, teach, empower, and slowly make them like Jesus. To know him is to discover that the Christian life is not a lonely imitation of a distant Lord, but a shared life with a present God who has moved in to stay. That is the difference between a religion you carry and a Person who carries you.
